newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan opposition closer to endorsing poll boycott.
newsitem.headline: Jordan opposition closer to endorsing poll boycott.

text.p: Jordan's Islamist and secular opposition parties are edging towards endorsing a call by the influential Moslem Brotherhood to pull out of November parliamentary elections, opposition figures said on Tuesday.

They said members of the Brotherhood's Islamic Action Front (IAF) political arm and its partners in a broad opposition coalition had expressed growing support for a boycott to protest what they see as government moves to sideline them.

"The Brotherhood has ended the reluctance of the general opposition to boycott," said Salem al-Nahas, head of the Jordan People's Democratic Party. "It has ignited the option of the complete boycott. All the opposition parties will follow."

Analysts say an all-out boycott would deal a serious blow to Jordan's nascent democracy under King Hussein, who unlike many Arab leaders has so far accommodated the mainly Islamic opposition within mainstream politics.
The Islamist Action Front itself has not declared absolutely whether it will put up candidates.
Some IAF members, who won a fifth of parliamentary seats at the last elections, say a boycott would harm them, curbing Islamist influence and giving the government a free hand.
But Nahas, who attended an IAF meeting on Monday with 10 other parties, said only one -- the communists -- protested the boycott call. Five were firmly in favour, the rest undecided.
His own party formally announced on Tuesday it was boycotting the elections and professional union heads said they were urging their members not to stand as candidates or vote.

Dentists' chief Saeed Abu Mezer said if union members, who number tens of thousands, heeded the call a large chunk of eligible voters -- 1.46 million were registered for the 1993 elections -- would stay away.
The Brotherhood says successive governments have marginalised parliament and the opposition since Jordan's 1993 elections, its first multi-party elections for decades.
"The Brotherhood assessment is that they are no longer part of the state. This is the main thing which pushed them to take this action," Nahas said.

It announced it would reconsider its boycott call only if the government revoked a raft of "interim" laws, issued without being passed through parliament, and offered guarantees about political freedoms.
The government dismissed the Brotherhood demands as illogical and said elections would go ahead regardless.
Analysts say if the two sides do not come to a compromise, Jordan's eight-year experiment with democracy will take a big leap backwards.

"I don't think the government is capable of realising the danger of this step," said Hani Hourani, head of the pro-democracy New Jordan Centre and a supporter of opposition participation in the elections.
"It puts our political life at a turning point. If the opposition decide not to participate, especially the Moslem Brotherhood, it will not be a pluralistic election," he said.
"This will be a big disaster and show the government and the whole world that our democracy is not working normally."
Columnist Rami Khouri, writing in the English- language Jordan Times, said the opposition and the government were Siamese twins who could survive only if they worked together.
"A series of healthy, constructive political compromises is out there begging to be seized by more thoughtful and mature people," he wrote.
"We should remember that the world is watching us as we deal with this first major crisis of our modern but young democratisation process."

In the last elections in 1993 the Islamic Action Front won 16 of 80 seats in a parliament filled by small pro-government parties and tribal representatives. Together with other opposition members they sometimes mustered a voting bloc of 23.

But they failed to block ratification of Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, which the opposition want cancelled, and supporters of the boycott said it was time to pull out of a parliament which they said they could not influence.
